senses.d: A paved footpath located at the side of a road, for the use of pedestrians.
ex: Stay on the sidewalk.
Morning commuters in parts of Texas, Oklahoma and Arkansas discovered slick sidewalks and icy roadways Monday.

senses.d: Any paved footpath, even if not located at the side of a road.

From hacera, from facera, from facero, from Latin faciarius, from faciēs (“face”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *andagĭne. Possibly from Latin indāgō (“encirclement”).
From banca (“bench”) + -eta (diminutive suffix). The sense of sidewalk comes from the platforms, like low benches, which were used for walking on streets aside houses.

pt:calçada.gl: a cobbled street for pedestrian usage

ety.text: From Vulgar Latin calciāta (“paved road”), feminine of calciātus (“paved with limestone”), from Latin calcō (“trample”), from Latin calx (“limestone”). Cognate with Galician and Spanish calzada and French chaussée.
Deverbal from passear (“to take a trip”), from passo (“step”). Compare Sicilian passiju, Spanish paseo.

Proto-Indo-European *seh₁-der. Proto-Germanic *sīdaz Proto-Germanic *sīdǭ Old English sīde Middle English side English side From Middle English side, from Old English sīde (“side, flank”), from Proto-Germanic *sīdǭ (“side, flank, edge, shore”), derived from *sīdaz, probably from Proto-Indo-European *seh₁- (“long, lasting”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian Siede (“side”), West Frisian side (“side”), Dutch zijde, zij (“side”), German Low German Sied (“side”), German Seite (“side”), Danish, Norwegian Bokmål, and Norwegian Nynorsk side (“side”), Swedish sida (“side”).

ety.text: From Middle English side, syde, syd, from Old English sīd (“wide, broad, spacious, ample, extensive, vast, far-reaching”), from Proto-West Germanic *sīd, from Proto-Germanic *sīdaz (“drooping, hanging, low, excessive, extra”), from Proto-Indo-European *sēy- (“to send, throw, drop, sow, deposit”). Cognate with obsolete Dutch zijd (“wide, vast”), Low German sied (“low”), Swedish sid (“long, hanging down”), Icelandic síður (“low hanging, long”).

senses.d: A bounding straight edge of a two-dimensional shape.
ex: A square has four sides.

senses.d: A flat surface of a three-dimensional object; a face.
ex: A cube has six sides.
He said, “Where we’re at right now was back in 2008 all covered with ice. From here to there at the side, the glacier shrank about 20 to 30 meters.”

senses.d: One half (left or right, top or bottom, front or back, etc.) of something or someone.
ex: Which side of the tray shall I put it on?  The patient was bleeding on the right side.

senses.d: A region in a specified position with respect to something.
ex: Meet me on the north side of the monument.

senses.d: The portion of the human torso usually covered by the arms when they are not raised; the areas on the left and right between the belly or chest and the back.
ex: Meronyms: flank, loin; latus, lumbus
I generally sleep on my side.

senses.d: One surface of a sheet of paper (used instead of "page", which can mean one or both surfaces.)
ex: John wrote 15 sides for his essay!

senses.d: One possible aspect of a concept, person, or thing.
ex: Look on the bright side.
She has a mean side (to her).

senses.d: One set of competitors in a game.
ex: Which side has kick-off?

senses.d: A sports team.
A group of morris dancers who perform together.
Being on the left or right, or toward the left or right; lateral.
ex: One mighty squadron with a side wind sped.

senses.d: Indirect; oblique; incidental.
ex: a side issue; a side view or remark
The law hath no side respect to their persons.

senses.d: To ally oneself, be in an alliance, usually with "with" or rarely "in with"
ex: Which will you side with, good or evil?
All side in parties, and begin the attack.

senses.d: To lean on one side.
To be or stand at the side of; to be on the side toward.
ex: His blind eye that syded Paridell.

senses.d: To suit; to pair; to match.
To work (a timber or rib) to a certain thickness by trimming the sides.
To furnish with a siding.
ex: to side a house

senses.d: To provide with, as a side or accompaniment.
ex: Entrees are sided with a generous portion of vegetables, and some include little surprises […]
A chocolate cakelette, caramel percolating from its warm top, is sided with peanut butter chantilly cream.

senses.d: Wide; large; long, pendulous, hanging low, trailing; far-reaching.
ex: Hiz gooun had syde sleeuez dooun to midlegge, slit from the shooulder too the hand, & lined with white cotten.

senses.d: Far; distant.
Widely; wide; far.
To clear, tidy or sort.
ex: Meanwhile I have plenty to employ me, in siding drawers and locked places, which I left in the disgracefullest confusion ;
Now side everything away. The medicines too —put them in the cupboard.

Inherited from Middle French equippe, from Middle French equipper, esquiper. More at French équiper.
Deverbal from squadrare + -a. May correspond to a Vulgar Latin *exquadra, from *exquadro, exquadrāre, from Latin ex- + quadrō, from quadrus. Compare French équerre.
Borrowed from French équipe, with unexpected change in gender. Compare with Catalan equip (with the same gender), Portuguese equipa, French équipe, and English equip.

Borrowed from English team.
From side + -ways.

senses.d: Moving or directed toward one side.
ex: Giving Mary a sideways glance, he said,[…].
He gave the ball a sideways kick.

senses.d: Positioned sideways (with a side to the front).
ex: There was a stack of papers in front of each seat at the table, but each stack was sideways.

senses.d: Neither moving upward nor moving downward.
ex: Once we get out of this sideways economy, our figures will more accurately reflect what we're truly capable of.

senses.d: In conflict (with); not compatible (with).
ex: He was constantly getting sideways with his boss till he got fired.

senses.d: With a side to the front.
ex: He builds houses sideways, with the front door on the side.

senses.d: Towards one side.
ex: A bishop moves only diagonally; a rook, only sideways, forward, and back.
He looked sideways at the new arrival, wondering who she was.

senses.d: Askance; sidelong.
Neither upward nor downward.
ex: The economy has been moving sideways for several months now.

senses.d: Not as planned; towards a worse outcome.
ex: We realized the project could go sideways very quickly if we didn't get the sales and marketing people on our side.
It feels like the probability of something going sideways here is higher.

Proto-Indo-European *seh₁-der. Proto-Germanic *sīdaz Proto-Germanic *sīdǭ Old English sīde Middle English side English side English -ing English siding From side + -ing (“derivative noun, having the quality of”).

senses.d: A building material which covers and protects the sides of a house or other building.
ex: Ugh. If there's one thing I can't stand it's cheesy vinyl siding.

senses.d: A second, relatively short length of track just to the side of a railroad track, joined to the main track by switches at one or both ends, used either for loading or unloading freight, storing trains or other rail vehicles; or to allow two trains on a same track to meet (opposite directions) or pass (same direction) (the latter sense is probably an American definition).
ex: They slept where they could, sometimes in an empty truck on a siding near the station, sometimes in a cart behind a warehouse; [...]

grp.label: material to cover the sides of a building
